context_blurb:
Every living thing is built of cells, most of them far too small to see. What we know of them began with lenses: a Dutch cloth seller's tiny ones in the 1600s, German scientists' microscopes in the 1800s, then a microscope that sees with electrons.

Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a cloth seller in Delft, built his own microscopes, each a single tiny lens set in a brass plate. The compound microscopes of the time, such as Robert Hooke's, used two lenses in a row, yet Leeuwenhoek's one lens showed sharper detail. Every lens of that time blurred the picture a little and fringed it with colour, and in a microscope with two lenses the flaws of both added up. His lenses were tiny, most under 3 millimetres across, and for a microscope the smaller the lens, the more it magnifies: his best made things look over 250 times bigger, Hooke's about 50.

In 1676 Leeuwenhoek told the Royal Society in London, a club of leading scientists, that a drop of pepper water swarmed with over a million tiny living things. Some of its Fellows doubted him. Witnesses, drawings and counts all rested on Leeuwenhoek and his lenses, and he kept his methods secret. The doubters needed an observation that did not depend on him: one of their own Fellows seeing the creatures for himself, through a microscope of his own. After two failures, Robert Hooke did just that in November 1677, and the Society's records say no doubt was left.

In 1683 Leeuwenhoek stirred a pasty white film from his own teeth into rainwater that held no living things, and the mix swarmed with tiny moving ones. They were bacteria, and his letter about them is often counted as the first clear sighting of bacteria. His Dutch word for such creatures meant little animals; his English translators made it animalcules. They were single cells, not tiny many-celled animals like mites.

Plant cells are easy to pick out, since a thick wall surrounds each one, and in 1838 the German plant scientist Matthias Schleiden concluded that all plants are built of cells. An animal cell has no stiff wall, so its edges are faint. Schleiden held the nucleus, a cell's control centre, to be its most important part. Theodor Schwann reasoned that if plants and animals were built alike, the nucleus should turn up in animal tissue too, and his microscope found nuclei in tissue after tissue. In 1839 he showed that animal bodies are made of cells as well.

Both men thought new cells formed out of a fluid, the way crystals do. Robert Remak found the truth first. He watched the red blood cells of chicken embryos, chicks still growing in the egg, pinch in two, and published it in 1852, but few noticed. In 1855 Rudolf Virchow, a German doctor who had at first doubted that cells divide, made the idea famous with the Latin motto omnis cellula e cellula: every cell from a cell. His essay never named Remak, and the historian Paul Weindling says Virchow plagiarised Remak's idea, passing it off as his own. That rule is now part of cell theory.

In 1931, in Berlin, Max Knoll and Ernst Ruska built the first electron microscope. It uses a beam of electrons instead of light, so it can show far finer detail. Most viruses are about a hundredth the size of a bacterium, beyond the reach of any light microscope, and the first pictures of one, the tobacco mosaic virus, came from an electron microscope in 1939.

A school microscope is a compound microscope: the eye looks through the eyepiece, and objective lenses of different strengths turn into place on the nosepiece, above a slide clipped to the stage. The diaphragm, under the stage, opens and closes to let more or less light up through the slide, and closing it a little cuts the glare so pale cells stand out.

The coarse knob makes big moves, right for finding a cell at low power, but a high-power lens sits so close to the slide that one big turn can crash it into the glass, scratching the lens and cracking the slide. The fine knob makes the small moves high power needs, and focusing never changes the magnification. The objective makes an enlarged picture of the cells, and the eyepiece enlarges that picture again, so the total magnification is the two lenses' numbers multiplied together.
